extracted.intended_audience: comedians, humor writers, performers, and students/scholars of humor and audience dynamics
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist and conceptual guide for evaluating or crafting jokes that rely on in-group/out-group dynamics, focusing on speaker identity, audience trust, and the social functions of denigrating targets. Useful for performers and writers to judge whether a line will land or backfire with a given audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidarity Function
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor denigrating an out-group reinforces in-group solidarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes invoke imaginary enemies — spouses, mothers-in-law, politicians, bosses — to summon belonging. Use such jokes to bond the in-group by sharing mockery; be aware this is a primary social function of out-group humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity-of-Speaker Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Who delivers the joke matters significantly: a joke about a group is funnier, less offensive, more acceptable when made by an in-group member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a gay joke from a gay person is perceived differently than the same joke from a straight person; an Asian joke from an Asian person > from someone outside. Race jokes from same-race comedians are often considered acceptable while identical content from outsiders is considered offensive. Evaluate speaker identity relative to the target group before delivering/transmitting the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust Relationship (Comedian–Audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is a trust transaction in which audience extends benefit of the doubt and comedian earns the ability to transgress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust is earned through identity, history, and persona; it enables transgression — without trust, the same line reads as hostile. Trust both allows humor to land and can be built reciprocally by successful jokes; conversely, failed humor damages trust. Consider the comedian's track record and persona when predicting audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live Joke Performance Dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: In live performance the room defines who is in; out-group persons may be 'present' as subjects even when physically absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-group scenarios are 'haunted by out-group persons.' The spatial/situational makeup of the room affects who counts as in-group or out-group. Assess the live audience composition and the social context (who's in the room, who is implied) when choosing or timing a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic Uses of In-Group/Out-Group Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes can be used strategically for different social functions: solidarity, hierarchy, identity-indexing, critique, and self-mockery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cases: solidarity — bond the in-group via shared mockery; hierarchy — establish status within a group; identity-indexing — signal who you are to an audience; critique ('punch up') — target power structures; self-mockery — reveal in-group flaws to disarm outside critique. Evaluate the intended strategic effect and whether the chosen target and speaker identity align with that aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item: Who is the joke's in-group / out-group?
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which people count as in-group and which as out-group for the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the social targets and beneficiaries of the joke explicitly. Determine whether the joke targets an out-group and which audience members will interpret themselves as in-group; misidentification can cause harm or misfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item: Does the comedian have in-group standing?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the comedian is perceived as a member of the joke's in-group relative to the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the comedian has in-group standing, similar content is more likely to be judged funny and less offensive. If not, the same content may be interpreted as hostile. Consider background, identity signals, and established persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item: Has the comedian earned audience trust?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the performer has an established trust relationship with the audience that permits transgressive material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust is earned through prior interaction, demonstrated persona, and history. Even with in-group standing, lack of trust means transgression will be read as aggression rather than playful. Factor in context, prior rapport, and track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item: Does the joke build or break solidarity?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the joke strengthens in-group bonds or damages them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some jokes reinforce belonging and mutual identity; others alienate or divide. Consider short- and long-term social effects: a single laugh may harm long-term trust or group cohesion if the joke is perceived as exclusionary or hostile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item: Does the audience identity match the comedian's intended audience?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the actual audience aligns with the audience the comedian assumes when crafting or delivering the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misalignment between intended and actual audience identity leads to misreadings and offense. Always gauge audience composition and expectations; tailor material or introduce contextual framing to reduce mismatch.
